meta.title: The AI Curve
meta.subtitle: Thirteen ideas. Four chapters. One direction.
meta.source: assets/temp/The AI Curve - Keynote Trend Lines.pptx
meta.dataNote: Figures and claims are transcribed from the supplied October 2026 deck, not independently reverified. Intermediate values recovered from plotted geometry are rounded. Smooth connecting curves are visual guides, not additional observations or forecasts.

scenes.title: The AI|curve.
scenes.description:
A new shape of possibility.
Told through the lines that matter.
notes: This is a story about direction, not a catalogue of products. Capability is rising, the cost of intelligence is falling, and adoption is moving from experimentation into everyday work.
Read each curve as a leadership question: what becomes possible for our organization when this trend continues?
scenes.takeaway: Plan for the curve, not the snapshot.

scenes.title: One story.|Four movements.
scenes.description: From what AI can do, to what we choose to do with it.
notes: Start with the underlying economics and capability shift. Follow the investment and demand signal. Then move from adoption to the redesign of work.
The source deck's two demand charts and three platform panels each have their own scene here, so every visual has room to breathe.
scenes.takeaway: Capability. Investment. Adoption. Reinvention.

scenes.title: AI's working day|is getting longer.
scenes.description: From minutes of work to hours of autonomy.
scenes.metricLabel: days to double task length, since 2024
scenes.insight: Keep people on direction and judgement. Prepare workflows for longer, bounded delegation.

chart.title: Length of task AI completes independently
chart.subtitle: Human-expert minutes · 50% success rate · logarithmic scale

scenes.source: METR · Time Horizon 1.1 (29 Jan 2026); Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks (Mar 2025).
scenes.caveat: Benchmark tasks at 50% success, not a guarantee of reliable autonomous work. Log scale.
notes: The measured horizon is the length of a task, expressed in the time a human expert would need, that a model completes with 50% probability. It is not the time the model runs, and not a promise of production reliability.
The deck reports a doubling time of about 89 days since 2024. The leadership implication is to design adaptable workflows, not to assume every task can already be delegated.
scenes.takeaway: Plan for the curve, with explicit reliability gates.

scenes.title: Intelligence is becoming|radically cheaper.
scenes.description: The same capability. A very different price.
scenes.metricLabel: lower GPT-4-level inference price in the source comparison
scenes.insight: Yesterday's unit economics should not set tomorrow's ambition.

chart.title: Cheapest price for a fixed capability
chart.subtitle: USD per million tokens · logarithmic scale

scenes.source: Epoch AI · LLM inference price trends (Mar 2025); Stanford HAI AI Index 2025; a16z · LLMflation.
scenes.caveat: Fixed-capability inference pricing, not total solution cost. Intermediate plotted values rounded.
notes: The source compares the cheapest available inference price at a fixed capability level, rather than the price of one unchanged model. Its GPT-4-level endpoints are $37.50 and $0.12 per million tokens.
That is about a 312-fold reduction. Governance, integration, evaluation and human oversight still cost money; lower inference cost is not the same as a free implementation.
scenes.takeaway: Revisit the economics. Keep the operating costs in view.

scenes.title: This is infrastructure.|Not just a software cycle.
scenes.description: A build-out measured in years, against projects measured in decades.
scenes.insightTitle: The infrastructure is being built. Your advantage is what you build on it.
scenes.insight: Data, processes and people become the differentiators.

chart.title: AI build-out versus historic megaprojects
chart.subtitle: Cumulative USD billions · years since start

scenes.source: Company 10-Ks via CRE42; F. Moorhouse / Forethought megaproject compilation via GIGAZINE (May 2026).
scenes.caveat: Big Tech includes all capex, not AI alone. Historical totals inflation-adjusted; grey paths show average pace. 2026 is guidance.
notes: These are not like-for-like project budgets. The source compares nominal Big Tech capital expenditure with inflation-adjusted historic megaproject totals, using straight lines for the historic average pace.

The cumulative Big Tech trajectory follows the supplied source chart, starting from a zero origin. The dashed terminal segment includes guidance, not completed expenditure. Treat the comparison as a sense of scale, not a precise economic ranking.
scenes.takeaway: The strategic question moves from infrastructure availability to organizational readiness.

scenes.title: Ten times the investment.|Seven years.
scenes.description: The annual commitment behind the curve.
scenes.insightTitle: Build skills before the capacity arrives.
scenes.insight: Platform choices, data foundations and people need a head start.

chart.title: Alphabet + Amazon + Meta + Microsoft
chart.subtitle: Annual capital expenditure · USD billions, nominal

scenes.source: Company 10-K filings via CRE42 · Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft.
scenes.caveat: All capital expenditure, not AI-only spending. G = guidance, not an actual result.
notes: The source reports $72 billion in 2019 and $733 billion guided for 2026. The ratio is just over ten times.
This includes the companies' entire capital expenditure. It should not be described as a pure measure of AI investment or proof of a return on that investment.
scenes.takeaway: The scale of commitment is clear. The return still has to be earned.

scenes.title: Demand is moving|into production.
scenes.description: Microsoft Cloud revenue has more than doubled.
scenes.metricLabel: Microsoft Cloud revenue in Q1 FY27
scenes.insight: Move the conversation from the number of pilots to the outcomes in production.

chart.title: Microsoft Cloud revenue
chart.subtitle: USD billions per quarter · fiscal quarters

scenes.source: Microsoft Investor Relations · quarterly metrics FY24 Q4, FY25 Q4, FY27 Q1, as cited in the deck.
scenes.caveat: Cloud revenue is broader than AI revenue. Intermediate values recovered from the source chart.
notes: This is the first of two visuals on source slide 7. It shows Microsoft Cloud quarterly revenue, not revenue attributable only to AI.
The source endpoints are $30.3 billion and $63.9 billion. Intermediate plotted values have been recovered from the original chart geometry and rounded to one decimal.
scenes.takeaway: Growing demand is a signal to scale proven outcomes, not to skip evaluation.

scenes.title: Bigger.|And accelerating.
scenes.description: A separate lens: Azure's year-on-year growth rate.
scenes.metricLabel: Azure year-on-year growth in Q1 FY27
scenes.insight: Read the revenue curve and the growth curve together, without conflating them.
scenes.source: Microsoft Investor Relations; CNBC for restated FY24 Q1-Q3 Azure metrics, as cited in the deck.
scenes.caveat: Year-on-year Azure growth, not Microsoft Cloud growth. Source chart transcription; not independently verified.
notes: This is the second visual on source slide 7, separated to make the distinction legible. Azure year-on-year growth and Microsoft Cloud absolute revenue are different measures.
The curve is not uninterrupted acceleration: it dips and recovers. The source shows a rise to 48% at the final point.
scenes.takeaway: A stronger demand signal. Not a substitute for your own business case.

scenes.title: One billion people.|Every week.
scenes.description: A consumer habit is becoming a workplace expectation.
scenes.metricLabel: ChatGPT weekly active users in the source deck
scenes.insight: Give them a governed way to bring that capability into work.
scenes.source: OpenAI statements via TechCrunch (Feb 2026) and press (Aug 2026); NBER w34255; Reuters / UBS.
scenes.caveat: Weekly active users; do not confuse with the 100M monthly-user launch milestone.
notes: The line shows weekly active users, as presented in the supplied deck. The commonly quoted 100 million users in two months is a different launch-era monthly-user measure and is deliberately not plotted as a weekly data point.
The organizational opportunity is not just access. It is approved tools, clear boundaries, training and a way to turn individual experimentation into repeatable value.
scenes.takeaway: Make governed work AI at least as usable as personal AI.

scenes.title: A licence is not a habit.|Daily use is.
scenes.description: Adoption gets deeper, not just wider.
scenes.metricLabel: of US employees report some AI use
scenes.insightTitle: Measure active behaviour, not provisioned seats.
scenes.insight: Invest in managers and champions who turn occasional use into confident habits.

chart.title: US employees using AI at work
chart.subtitle: Percentage of employees · frequency groups overlap, they are not additive

scenes.source: Gallup · AI in the Workplace indicator (2023-May 2026); Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (Mar 2026).
scenes.caveat: US employee survey, not enterprise adoption. Daily users are included in weekly and any-use groups.
notes: The nested frequency groups should never be stacked or summed. Fifteen percent daily users sit within thirty percent weekly-or-more users, which sit within fifty-two percent any-use employees.
This is why a line comparison is more honest than a stacked area. The strategic question is what helps occasional use become a useful, safe working habit.
scenes.takeaway: The useful KPI is sustained, outcome-producing use.

scenes.title: The early majority|is arriving.
scenes.description: But a changing survey question matters to the story.
scenes.metricLabel: US firms using AI, under the broader question
scenes.insight: Build the capabilities that make it work better for your business.

chart.title: US firms reporting AI use
chart.subtitle: Census BTOS · percent of firms · last two weeks

scenes.source: US Census Bureau · BTOS, CES-WP-24-16R; Census story (May 2026); Anthropic Economic Index.
scenes.caveat: Nov 2025 question broadened to any business function. The break is intentional: not a clean like-for-like growth series.
notes: The original source places its 9.7% point before the November 2025 question change, then 19.8% after it. This adaptation deliberately does not connect those points across the definition break.

The source's rhetorical increase from one in thirty to one in five mixes survey definitions. We preserve the reported values but make the comparability limit visible rather than implying an uninterrupted adoption curve.
scenes.takeaway: Enterprise use is spreading. Compare definitions before comparing growth.

scenes.title: A head start.|Not a finish line.
scenes.description: Nordic enterprises are setting Europe's adoption pace.
scenes.insightTitle: Convert the regional lead into scaled value.
scenes.insight: A lead in adoption only matters if it changes business outcomes.

chart.title: Enterprises using AI technologies
chart.subtitle: Percent of enterprises with 10+ employees · timeline trails + 2025 ranking

scenes.source: Eurostat · Use of AI in enterprises (Jan 2025 and Dec 2025 releases).
scenes.caveat: Enterprises with 10+ employees. Denmark / Sweden 2023 values derived in the source; no missing years invented.
notes: These are enterprise adoption percentages, not population use. The underlying population is businesses with at least ten employees.
Denmark and Sweden's 2023 values were derived in the source from reported year-on-year changes. Finland's trail begins in 2024 because the supplied graph does not plot an earlier observation.
scenes.takeaway: Turn adoption advantage into operating advantage.

scenes.title: Value follows diffusion.|Not just invention.
scenes.description: The advantage goes to those who spread capability.
scenes.metricLabel: global working-age population using generative AI
scenes.insightTitle: Make broad, skilled adoption a strategy.
scenes.insight: Access is the beginning. Confident use is the multiplier.

chart.title: Working-age population using generative AI
chart.subtitle: Percent of people aged 15-64 · reporting periods, not equally spaced dates

scenes.source: Microsoft AI Economy Institute · AI Diffusion Reports (Jan, May, Sep 2026).
scenes.caveat: Population adoption estimates, not enterprise penetration. Missing country-period values are not backfilled.
notes: The chart switches from enterprise adoption to working-age population diffusion. These measures are deliberately kept separate.
Sweden and the US begin at H2 2025 because no H1 observation is shown for them in the source graph. The periods have unequal duration, so this is a period comparison, not a growth-rate calculation.
scenes.takeaway: Spread capability widely enough for the economy of work to change.

scenes.title: The crossing point|is not the whole story.
scenes.description: Delegation rises. Collaboration remains essential.
scenes.metricLabel: automation in business API use, Aug 2025
scenes.insightTitle: Redesign processes, not just individual tasks.
scenes.insight: Keep judgement and oversight central as delegation grows.

chart.title: How people use Claude
chart.subtitle: Percent of Claude.ai conversations · separate API statistic uses a different population

scenes.source: Anthropic Economic Index · Feb 2025, Sep 2025, Jan 2026 reports.
scenes.caveat: Automation overtook augmentation in Aug 2025, but not Nov 2025. Directive is a subtype, not an additive category.
notes: The important nuance is visible in the final data point: augmentation returns to 52%, versus 45% automation, in November. The deck's crossing-point story should not be presented as an irreversible takeover.
The 77% business API figure is a separate population from Claude.ai conversations. Directive usage is a subtype and must not be added to the other lines.
scenes.takeaway: Design for both collaboration and bounded delegation.

scenes.title: AI is leaving|the IT department.
scenes.description: Coding started the wave. Other functions are joining it.
scenes.metricLabel: education's share of Claude.ai tasks in the source's latest education observation
scenes.insightTitle: Put an owner in every function.
scenes.insight: Look for value in service, sales, finance, HR and the work between them.

chart.title: Share of Claude.ai tasks by occupation group
chart.subtitle: Percent of conversations · each line ends at its last supplied observation

scenes.source: Anthropic Economic Index · Feb, Mar, Sep 2025; Jan, Mar 2026. BCG Applied AI Index 2026 also cited by the deck.
scenes.caveat: Share of observed Claude.ai conversations, not market share or total spending. Observation dates differ by series.
notes: Computer and mathematical tasks remain the largest of the shown groups, while education and management gain share.

The education series stops before the others in the original visual. It is not extrapolated. The source's separate statement about spending outside enterprise IT is not encoded as conversation-share data.
scenes.takeaway: AI ownership belongs across the business, not in one department.

scenes.title: The developer frontier|is compounding.
scenes.description: Start where the working habit is already changing.
scenes.metricLabel: GitHub Copilot users reported in the source
scenes.insightTitle: From a tool to a working system.
scenes.insight: Connect individual assistance to repeatable engineering outcomes.

chart.title: GitHub Copilot users
chart.subtitle: Millions · source earnings-call disclosures · zero baseline

scenes.source: Microsoft earnings calls FY25 Q3-FY27 Q1 (Apr 2025-Oct 2026); some interim figures via third-party transcripts.
scenes.caveat: Users, not paid seats. Source point spacing retained; exact interim dates not specified in this adaptation.
notes: The source's first platform panel uses GitHub Copilot users. It grows from fifteen to fifty million across the shown disclosures.
Do not compare this absolute number directly with paid seats or customer organizations in the next panels. Each is a different population with its own zero-based scale.
scenes.takeaway: Move from adoption volume to engineering impact.

scenes.title: The knowledge-work|frontier is scaling.
scenes.description: Paid seats tell a different part of the adoption story.
scenes.insightTitle: Seats create access. Habits create value.
scenes.insight: Tie rollout to role-specific workflows, evaluation and measurable outcomes.

chart.title: Microsoft 365 Copilot paid seats
chart.subtitle: Millions · source earnings-call disclosures · zero baseline

scenes.source: Microsoft earnings calls FY25 Q3-FY27 Q1 (Apr 2025-Oct 2026), as cited in the source deck.
scenes.caveat: Paid seats, not active users. Disclosure order retained; the source panel labels 2025-2026.
notes: This is the source's second platform panel, separated from users and customer counts. The source reports paid seats rising from fifteen to thirty million.
Paid seats are an access measure. They should not be described as daily active usage, realized productivity or a verified business return.
scenes.takeaway: Turn access into a habit, and the habit into a measurable outcome.

scenes.title: The builder frontier|is widening.
scenes.description: More organizations are building on the platform.
scenes.metricLabel: Foundry customer organizations in the source
scenes.insight: The destination is one governed operating model, not disconnected experiments.

chart.title: Foundry customers
chart.subtitle: Thousands · source earnings-call disclosures · zero baseline

scenes.source: Microsoft earnings calls FY25 Q3-FY27 Q1 (Apr 2025-Oct 2026), as cited in the source deck.
scenes.caveat: Customer organizations, not users or seats. Platform panels use different units and independent scales.
notes: This is the source's third platform panel, measured in customer organizations. Seventy, one hundred and one hundred twenty thousand are the three plotted disclosures.
The broader Frontier Firm story connects platforms to data, governance and redesigned workflows. Platform growth alone does not demonstrate that every customer has achieved that operating model.
scenes.takeaway: Build an operating capability, not a collection of pilots.

scenes.title: Where will you sit|on the curve?
scenes.description:
Capability up. Cost down. Adoption up.
The next move is an organizational choice.
notes: Every trend in the source deck points to a larger set of possibilities, but no curve makes the leadership decision for us.
Choose one valuable workflow, set a measurable outcome, establish boundaries and ownership, and build the organizational muscle to learn from the result.
scenes.takeaway: Start with one outcome. Build for the curve.

scenes.title: A story with|its sources attached.
scenes.description: Original references from the supplied deck. Figures are source-deck claims, not independently verified live statistics.
notes: These are the references provided by the author of the source deck. Refer to the scene-specific source and caveat for the population, metric, timeframe and comparability limits.
Smooth curves are visual guides between source observations. They are not forecasts. Guidance is explicitly dashed and survey breaks are not joined.
scenes.takeaway: Keep the evidence and its limits in the story.
